summary:
Article 347-1 of the Cameroonian penal code criminalises same-sex conduct and carries a sentence of up to five years' imprisonment. The 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations, replacing a colonial-era sodomy provision under which sentences ranged between six months and five years. Cameroon is one of 31 African countries that criminalise same-sex conduct, and a 2020 assessment described it as prosecuting consensual same-sex conduct more aggressively than almost any country in the world. Reporting places Cameroon among the states in Africa with the highest prosecution rates.

Trans women have been prosecuted on the basis of clothing and gender presentation. In February 2021 a court in Douala convicted Shakiro, a trans woman with a Facebook and YouTube following, and her friend Patricia, charging them with attempted homosexuality, public indecency and failing to carry identification. Both received the maximum statutory term of five years plus a fine of 200,000 CFA francs each. Defence lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu described the judgment as a political decision supported by no proof of any act, and an appeal was filed. The two women spent five months in prison before release pending appeal in 2021. Shakiro subsequently fled Cameroon to claim asylum abroad.

Appearance alone has served as the basis for prosecution. In November 2011 a Cameroonian court jailed Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome for five years after they were seen wearing women's clothes and ordering Baileys; the original judge cited their dress, speech and the drink as proof that they were gay. An appeals court acquitted both men on 9 January 2013, with defence lawyer Alice Nkom arguing the conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts, and Amnesty International welcoming the outcome. Jean-Claude Roger Mbede was arrested in 2011 for sending SMS messages to a male acquaintance and served a three-year sentence at Kondengui Central Prison. In November 2011 three young men received five years for oral sex in a parked car.

Human Rights Watch documented a sharp rise in violence against LGBTI people in 2022. From 9 March of that year security forces arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven, all of them victims of group attacks, over alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity; gendarmes beat two detainees. The organisation's researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi stated that the criminalisation law allows both civilians and security forces to abuse LGBTI people without consequence. Beatings of gay and trans people in public are reported as common.

The Law on Cybersecurity and Cybercrime (Law No. 2010/012, Article 83(1)) criminalises online same-sex sexual propositions with one to two years' imprisonment and fines of 500,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs, doubled where intercourse followed.

There is no legal gender recognition procedure and no documented name-change or identification and marker process; no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection covers gender identity or sexual orientation. Failure to carry identification was itself charged alongside the anti-homosexuality counts in the 2021 case against Shakiro and Patricia. A US State Department report noted harassment and extortion of gay and lesbian people by law enforcement and the use of false allegations to harass or extort.

Detention carries additional risk. Prisoners accused of homosexuality describe Douala's main prison as hell, and Kondengui Central Prison held Jean-Claude Roger Mbede for three years. Few lawyers are willing to defend people accused in homosexuality cases. Alternatives-Cameroon, an LGBTQ organisation, shut down after a police raid, removing a service base.

No Cameroonian visa policy, entry-refusal rule or border-admission procedure for LGBTQ travellers is described in the sources. The nearest material concerns outbound movement: in July 2010 the United Kingdom granted a gay Cameroonian man the right to claim asylum, prompting Minister of Communication Issa Tchiroma Bakary to argue that homosexuals are not prosecuted for private activities. In August 2011 a gay Cameroonian man was granted temporary immigration bail from the UK Border Agency after Air France refused to carry him to Yaoundé. In May 2012 the UK Border Agency sought to return asylum seeker Ediage Valerie Ekwedde, finding no credible evidence that he was gay. In May 2005 the government threatened medical examinations to prove homosexual activity among eleven men arrested at a nightclub.
